migrationNotes: SPINE: Sit in two rooms. First in Rochester in 1852 with Frederick Douglass, then at Gettysburg in 1863 with Abraham Lincoln, and in each one ask how the speaker earns trust, moves the audience and reasons, and how the speech fits the day on which it is given.

lesson.title: Ethos, pathos, logos and kairos

lead.text: Aristotle noticed that a speaker persuades through three channels at once, and he called them proofs. The first is ethos, the speaker's character and credibility. A listener trusts a mechanic who says “I have fixed engines for thirty years” before hearing anything else she says.

The second is pathos, the feeling a speech arouses in the people hearing it. “Picture your own child waiting at the school gate in the dark” works on pity and fear, and it does so with an image and no argument. The third is logos, the argument carried by the words themselves. “Three of the last five buses ran late and the timetable has not changed, so it will run late again” reasons from a fact to a consequence.

afterFigure.text: Real speeches mix all three, often inside one sentence. Reading well means asking of each part what it is working on: the speaker's standing, the listeners' feelings or the chain of reasoning. The name of the appeal follows from the answer.

model.source: An invented meeting of bus users

spans.text: I have ridden the number 9 to work for thirty years.
Picture your own child waiting at the school gate in the dark.
Three of the last five buses ran late and the timetable has not changed, so it will run late again.
Our coaches have trained county champions since 1998.
Picture a child swimming her first length, grinning at the far wall.
Pupils who join at six reach county standard by twelve, so starting early pays off.

lead.text: Ask whether the sentence reasons or moves, and who it speaks for.

On 5 July 1852, the day after Independence Day, Frederick Douglass stood up in Rochester, New York, to speak to an audience that had gathered to mark the nation's independence. Douglass had escaped from slavery as a young man and was by then a well-known speaker and writer. The people in the hall expected praise of the founders and of the republic.

A speaker in that position has an unusual problem. He must be heard as someone entitled to speak on the subject, and he is addressing people who see the day very differently from him. Whatever else his speech does, it has to settle first whose voice the audience is listening to.

afterFigure.text: His opening moves answer that problem. He sets himself apart from the audience's celebration and says so plainly, and the rest of the speech then rests on what that position allows him to say.

lead.text: Here are the first lines of the speech. Ask what gives Douglass the right to say them.

reveal.text: His standing as someone who lived what he describes is his proof. A speaker who builds trust in this way is relying on ethos.

spans.text: I am not included within the pale of this glorious anniversary!
This Fourth of July is yours, not mine.
You may rejoice, I must mourn.
As chair of this society for twelve years, I have signed every one of its accounts.

steps.headline: Name the appeals in: “As a lifelong farmer, I ask you to picture the empty field next spring.”

lead.text: One sentence can carry two appeals. Separate them by what each part works on.

workedSteps.text: Split the sentence by what each part works on.
“As a lifelong farmer” says who is speaking and why to trust her. That is ethos.
“Picture the empty field” asks you to feel a loss. That is pathos.

steps.headline: Name the appeal in Douglass's contrast between two outcomes of one sunlight.

lead.text: Douglass sets one sunlight against two outcomes. “Stripes” are the marks of the whip, placed beside the audience's own “life and healing”.

reveal.text: The contrast is physical, so the feeling is hard to avoid. The image is chosen to move the listeners, which is the work of pathos.

workedSteps.text: The audience hears two images side by side: one warm, one cruel.
The image is chosen to move the listeners. It offers no step of reasoning.
Name the appeal that works through the audience's feelings.

spans.text: The sunlight that brought life and healing to you, has brought stripes and death to me.
This Fourth of July is yours, not mine.

lead.text: Eleven years later, Abraham Lincoln spoke at the dedication of a cemetery on the Gettysburg battlefield. The battle had been fought in the first days of July, and in November the war was still going on. The main speaker that day was Edward Everett, who talked for about two hours. Lincoln followed with a speech that lasted around two minutes.

Lincoln opens with a date. “Four score and seven years ago” is an old-fashioned way of naming a number of years. A score is twenty. The phrase asks his listeners to count back from the day they stand in to the moment the nation began, and what he says about that moment is the base on which the rest of the speech is built.

afterFigure.text: A speaker who starts by pointing to the start of the nation gives the audience something to measure the present against. Working out where the phrase leads is the next task.

lead.text: Lincoln gave his speech in 1863. Count back through the years his opening phrase names.

reveal.text: The year belongs to the Declaration of Independence, so Lincoln rests the nation on its founding premise rather than on the Constitution. From that premise he argues what the war tests, which is logos.

spans.text: Four score and seven years ago our fathers brought forth on this continent, a new nation,
conceived in Liberty, and dedicated to the proposition that all men are created equal.
Now we are engaged in a great civil war,
testing whether that nation, or any nation so conceived and so dedicated, can long endure.

steps.headline: From a premise to a test

lead.text: Now the date can do its work. Lincoln points to the founding year and attaches a premise to it: the new nation was dedicated to the proposition that all men are created equal. The sentences that follow draw out what that premise implies, one step at a time, until he reaches the duty that falls on the people listening. That chain of reasoning is the logos of the speech.

Lincoln builds trust as well. He says “We have come to dedicate a portion of that field”, and the “we” makes the president one of the mourners. And he moves the audience with a plain phrase for the soldiers' sacrifice: “the last full measure of devotion”.

afterFigure.text: All three appeals are present in a few lines. Which one leads depends on the sentence, and a short speech can still use each of them.

spans.text: We have come to dedicate a portion of that field,
as a final resting place for those who here gave their lives that that nation might live.
that from these honored dead we take increased devotion to that cause for which they gave
the last full measure of devotion
Four score and seven years ago our fathers brought forth on this continent, a new nation, conceived in Liberty, and
dedicated to the proposition that all men are created equal.

steps.headline: The right words at the right moment

lead.text: Every speech is given somewhere, on some day, to people in a particular mood. The Greeks had a word for the right moment, kairos, which means an opportune time. Kairos is the fit between an argument and the occasion on which it is made. The same words can fall flat on one day and land on another.

A speaker can use the occasion in two ways. One is to make the occasion itself the subject, so that the audience's reason for being in the room becomes part of the argument. A coach three goals down at half time can say that this is exactly where the team has always found its best football. The other is to use the place as evidence, as when a speaker standing in a rebuilt school says that this is where the old building burned down. In both cases the argument would be weaker anywhere else.

afterFigure.text: Kairos is the hardest of the four to see, because it is not in the words alone. To find it, ask what the speech would lose if it were read on a different day in a different place.

model.source: An invented speech at a library opening

spans.text: We are standing where the old school burned down.
Tonight it is a reading room, and that says what this town values.
We are three goals down at half time, and that is exactly when this team has always found its best football.

lead.text: Douglass, invited to speak at a celebration of independence, asks his audience: “What to the American slave is your Fourth of July?”

reveal.text: He made the holiday's own meaning the argument. Lincoln did the same with the ground: “We are met on a great battle-field of that war” uses the place itself as evidence.

spans.text: What to the American slave is your Fourth of July?
I answer, a day that reveals to him, more than all other days in the year, the gross injustice and cruelty to which he is the constant victim.
We are met on a great battle-field of that war.

lesson.orientation: Trace the four appeals through Douglass's Fourth of July oration and Lincoln's Gettysburg Address, and see how each speech uses its moment.
lesson.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh text after a delay.

blocks.text: You are choosing a guide for a mountain trip, and each of three candidates gets one sentence to win you over. Before any of them has described a route or a price, you have already leaned towards one. You could not say exactly why, but the sentence told you something.

Speakers have long known that persuasion works through several channels at once. Some of it comes from who is speaking. Some comes from what the speaker makes you feel. Some comes from the reasoning, and some from the timing, since the same words can fall flat on one day and land on another. More than two thousand years ago Aristotle gave names to the first three, and later teachers added a fourth.
We will use those names to take apart two famous speeches, one by Frederick Douglass in 1852 and one by Abraham Lincoln in 1863.

intro.promise: By the end you'll name the appeal in a line of a speech and say how Douglass and Lincoln use their moment.

recap.keyIdea: Ethos, pathos and logos persuade through the speaker, the feelings and the argument. Kairos is how well a speech fits its moment.

blocks.text: You found the standing behind Douglass's “yours, not mine” and the image of “stripes and death” behind his contrast. You dated Lincoln's opening to 1776, and you saw why a holiday and a battlefield each suited the speech given there.

recap.nextHook: A speech persuades through its words as well as its reasoning, and the next lesson begins with Caesar's report of a victory, which people still remember as three short parts.

questions.prompt: Douglass tells his Rochester audience, “This Fourth of July is yours, not mine.” His right to say it rests on his own life as a man who had escaped slavery. Which of Aristotle's appeals works through the speaker's character and standing?
hints: The Greek word is the root of 'ethics'.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Ethos: the persuasive force of the speaker's character and credibility.

questions.onCorrect: Ethos: Douglass's own life as a man who had escaped slavery gives him the standing to say it.

misconceptions.feedback: Pathos works on the audience's feelings. Here the force comes from who is speaking.
Logos is the argument itself. Ask what gives Douglass the right to say these words.
Kairos is about timing. Ask what the speaker's own life lends to the claim.

questions.prompt: 'The sunlight that brought life and healing to you, has brought stripes and death to me.' The image of 'stripes and death' is aimed chiefly at the audience's feelings. Which appeal is this?
hints: The Greek root also gives English 'sympathy'.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Pathos: the appeal to the audience's emotions, here pity and shame.

questions.onCorrect: Pathos: “stripes and death” is chosen to move the hearers, and it makes the contrast physical.

misconceptions.feedback: Ethos is about the speaker's standing. This image is aimed at the hearers' feelings.
Nothing here is reasoned from premise to consequence. The image is chosen to move the audience.

questions.prompt: Lincoln spoke at Gettysburg in November 1863. 'Four score and seven years ago' points back to which year?
hints: Four score and seven is four twenties plus seven.
Subtract that number of years from the year of the speech.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Four score and seven is 4 × 20 + 7 = 87, and 1863 − 87 = 1776, the year of the Declaration of Independence.

questions.onCorrect: Four score and seven is 4 × 20 + 7 = 87, and 1863 − 87 takes the nation back to the Declaration.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the year of the speech. Subtract the years the phrase names.
That is how many years, not the year the phrase points back to.
That is the Constitution's year. Work out four twenties plus seven and take it from the year of the speech.

questions.prompt: Douglass delivered his attack on slavery at a celebration of American independence, the day after the Fourth of July. Which Greek term names a speaker's use of the right moment and occasion?
hints: It is the term often added to Aristotle's three appeals, and it means the opportune moment.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Kairos: the timeliness of a speech, the fit between argument and occasion.

questions.onCorrect: Kairos: the fit between a speech and the moment it is spoken in.

misconceptions.feedback: Those are Aristotle's three proofs. The question asks for the term about timing.

questions.prompt: Lincoln says the war is 'testing whether that nation, or any nation so conceived and so dedicated, can long endure.' He reasons from the nation's founding premise to what the war puts at stake. Which appeal is this chiefly?
hints: Look for the appeal named after the Greek for 'word' or 'reason'.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Logos: an appeal through reasoning from premise to consequence.

questions.onCorrect: Logos: Lincoln reasons from the nation's founding premise to what the war puts at stake.

misconceptions.feedback: Ethos concerns the speaker's character. This sentence reasons from a premise to a consequence.
The sentence moves from premise to consequence rather than stirring feeling.

questions.prompt: A charity letter opens: 'As a children's nurse for twenty years, I have seen what a missed vaccination can do.' Which appeal does the opening clause make first?
hints: Look at what the opening clause tells you about the writer.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Ethos: 'As a children's nurse for twenty years' establishes the writer's experience and credibility before anything else.

questions.onCorrect: Ethos: “As a children's nurse for twenty years” establishes experience and credibility first.

misconceptions.feedback: No emotional image has appeared yet. Look at what the opening clause says about the writer.
Nothing in the opening clause is about the moment or the occasion.

questions.prompt: You are choosing a mountain guide. Which sentence makes you trust her most before she says anything else?
hints: Which sentence tells you something about the speaker herself?

acceptedIdeas: “I have led this route forty times.”
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Her forty trips of the route earn trust.

choices.label: “I have led this route forty times.”

questions.onCorrect: Her record is what earns trust. A speaker's own experience can persuade before any argument begins.

misconceptions.feedback: That is a guess about the weather. It tells you nothing about her.
That is a fact anyone could state. It says nothing about her experience.

questions.prompt: “Because the budget has doubled while results have not, the programme should be reviewed.” Which Greek-named proof is at work: ethos, pathos or logos?
hints: Does the sentence reason, or does it move the audience?
questions.onCorrect: The sentence reasons from a fact to a conclusion. That is argument carried by the words themselves.

misconceptions.feedback: Nothing here is about who the speaker is or why she should be trusted.
No feeling is aroused. The sentence moves from a fact to a conclusion.

questions.prompt: Why does “As a lifelong farmer” count as ethos?

acceptedIdeas: It builds trust in the speaker's experience.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It tells the audience who is speaking and why to trust her.

choices.label: It builds trust in the speaker's experience.
It gives a reason for the policy.

questions.onCorrect: Ethos works through the speaker's character and standing. Experience is part of what makes her believable.

misconceptions.feedback: It arouses no fear. It tells you who is speaking.
A reason would be an argument. This phrase only says who the speaker is.

questions.prompt: “Think of the families who lost everything in the flood.” Which appeal does the sentence rely on?
hints: What does the sentence ask the audience to imagine?
questions.onCorrect: It asks the audience to picture a loss. That works on feeling, not on reasoning or on the speaker's standing.

misconceptions.feedback: The sentence says nothing about the speaker. Ask what it asks the audience to do.
No premise leads to a conclusion here. The sentence offers an image.

hints: The word means the right moment.

acceptedIdeas: Fitting an argument to its moment and place.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Fitting an argument to its moment and place.

choices.label: Fitting an argument to its moment and place.
Repeating a word at the start of clauses.
Arguing from a premise to a consequence.

questions.onCorrect: Kairos is the opportune moment: a speech fits its occasion and may use the place itself as evidence.

misconceptions.feedback: That is a figure of repetition, not a proof. Kairos is about timing.
That describes reasoning, not timing.
